1. The animation shows a grid of 307 tiles. Each tile appears to be one historical case, where a buyer and a renter who invests the difference are compared over a ten-year period. The sources listed are FHFA, BLS, Freddie Mac, and K. R. French (CRSP), which cover house prices, rents and inflation, mortgage rates, and stock returns. It is labeled "illustrative" and "US only, history, not a forecast."

2. In frames 1–3 every tile is dark and the caption asks "after the whole walk: how many lit?" In frames 4–6 some tiles light up. The count settles at "152 of 307 lit," and the label "about half" appears in the last frame. Lit tiles mean the buyer was ahead after ten years. Dark tiles mean the renter's investment pile was bigger.

3. Over the historical ten-year windows, buying beat renting and investing in about half the cases (152 of 307), and renting won in the other half. So neither choice won reliably. The lit tiles also come in clusters, which suggests the result depended on when the ten years started.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer would probably take away that "rent and invest the difference" is not a sure win. It beat buying about as often as it lost, so the outcome depends on circumstances and timing. That is my reading of the picture.

5. The advice in 4 is my own conclusion. The on-screen text only reports the count ("152 of 307 lit", "about half") and says it is history and not a forecast. It never tells the viewer what to do.
